To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we can use all the laboratory creep compaction time series data to estimate the stress exponent and activation volume, and (2) the stress exponent and effective stress exponent are strongly coupled.

(1) we have developed a robust Bayesian framework for integrating laboratory creep compaction measurements into fault zone models; (2) the resulting semiempirical creep law for fault zone porosity is robust and can be used to predict the time to failure of faults; and (3) this semiempirical fault zone model can be used to estimate the stress and temperature conditions in the fault zone, as well as to predict the fault zone porosity evolution during the interseismic phase.
(1) We have developed a new method to integrate laboratory creep compaction tests with numerical fault models to estimate the time to failure of an earthquake.

a new methodology for analyzing laboratory creep compaction and with the application of this methodology to a simple model of fault creep and earthquake rupture.
developing and applying an integrated methodology to obtain a quantitative law for fault zone evolution and then use that law in a fault model to predict rupture time and size.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we developed a new, robust, and efficient Bayesian inversion scheme for laboratory creep compaction tests and applied this technique to obtain a semiempirical law that can be used in fault zone modeling.
, by using a Bayesian approach, we can integrate laboratory compaction data into numerical fault models and obtain robust estimates of the rate of fault zone compaction.
we developed a robust Bayesian scheme for analyzing creep compaction experiments, which can be extended to any creep experiment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, with the Bayesian approach, one can use laboratory creep compaction tests to obtain quantitative estimates of the rate-controlling mechanisms in the fault zone.

the Bayesian inversion technique we developed is a powerful and general framework that can be applied to other laboratory compaction experiments, to other creep experiments on rocks, and even to other types of data, such as seismic data.

, by using a simple but physically motivated creep law to analyze creep compaction data, we can obtain a quantitative law for interseismic compaction, which can be incorporated into fault zone models to predict the time to failure.
